paper_title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.

Introduction 2 Few-step distillation seeks to make diffusion and flow models efficient without sacrificing generation quality (Esser et al., 2024; Ho et al., 2020). central challenge is to provide effective supervision when small number of student transitions must replace long teacher trajectory. Trajectory distillation learns from individual teacher trajectories (Song et al., 2023), whereas distribution matching allows the student to learn its own mapping by aligning student and teacher distributions (Luo et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023). Trajectory Distribution Matching (TDM) (Luo et al., 2025) extends this principle to intermediate transitions. Each step then learns partial denoising task, distributing supervision across the student trajectory and providing natural foundation for few-step distillation. For intermediate supervision to be effective, however, the training signal must faithfully reflect the distribution produced at each student step. In score-based methods, generator updates depend on the difference between teacher and student scores, requiring an auxiliary model to track the evolving student distribution. Intermediate transitions complicate this estimation: the students clean prediction and retained residual can be correlated, so perturbing its intermediate output generally differs from adding fresh Gaussian noise to the clean prediction. Our analysis of TDM shows why this distinction matters. Direct score estimation for the perturbed intermediate output can involve high-variance targets, while clean-target denoising can estimate different distribution from the one used for generator supervision. These observations motivate supervision that explicitly accounts for the students sampling process while allowing alternatives to its noisy-marginal score. Velocity targets offer this flexibility because they can be defined through paths with coupled endpoints (Liu et al., 2022), including dependencies inherited from student transition. We build on this flexibility to introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), framework for constructing student velocity fields and using their discrepancies from the teacher to guide distillation. Two prototypical velocity constructions are derived within VAD. A-form is rectified velocity that captures the expected clean prediction conditioned on perturbed sample; B-form is score-equivalent Gaussian velocity for the students perturbed distribution. The two forms thus express conditional-moment and distributional supervision within the same sampling process. vector-valued critic estimates the discrepancy between the chosen student field and the teacher field, and the generator learns from this discrepancy. The resulting framework provides unified perspective along two axes: which field to match and how to use its discrepancy to update the generator. With different generator updates, A-form connects to conditional moment matching, while B-form connects reverse-KL score distillation and Fisher-based field matching. These connections also clarify the relationship between an intended objective and its practical update. In particular, VAD explains the heuristic update of MMD (Salimans et al., 2024) and derives an alternative surrogate that recovers the exact gradient of MMDs desired objective. To use both types of supervision along few-step trajectory, we develop VA-TDM, retaining TDMs supervision of intermediate transitions. VA-TDM combines A-form and B-form through shared auxiliary backbone and blends complementary generator updates. Because samples from different student steps can follow different distributions even at the same noise level, we also condition field estimation on the transition being supervised. This provides different and accurate supervision signals among different steps. Figure 2 Human preference on video synthesis. Overall, our unified VAD framework connects existing distillation updates and derives new objectives, which VA-TDM combines with complementary velocity fields and transition-aware estimation for four-step generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance across backbones and tasks. On VA-TDM SD3.5-Medium, VA-TDM outperforms the compared few-step baselines across prompt following, image quality, and preference metrics, improving GenEval from TDMs 0.61 to 0.67 while increasing sample diversity. On FLUX.2-Klein-Base 4B, it surpasses the released four-step model, raising GenEval from 0.78 to 0.80 and OCR similarity from 0.64 to 0.69, with diversity measured by LPIPS improving from 0.47 to 0.56. Most notably, VA-TDM scales to MiniMax-H3 (MiniMax, 2026), state-of-the-art open-source audio-video model with 33B parameters. In our user study  (Fig. 2)  , VA-TDM wins 61.33% of comparisons against Fast-H3 at the same 4-NFE budget and achieves 45.53% preference rate against the 100-NFE teacher, compared with 24.67% for Fast-H3. Related Works Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration. Training-free methods for accelerating diffusion model sampling have progressed substantially (Li et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2024; Si et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2023). However, diffusion distillation remains essential for high-quality few-step generation. VA-TDM 12 Diffusion Distillation. Distilled models generate images from noise in one or few steps. Two main approaches transfer knowledge from pre-trained DMs: 1) Trajectory distillation (Luhman and Luhman, 2021; Meng et al., 2023; Salimans and Ho, 2022; Song and Dhariwal, 2024; Song et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2024) matches teacher ODE trajectories at the instance level, facing challenging instance-wise alignment and numerical errors in teacher PF-ODE solutions; 2) Distribution matching via score distillation (Liu et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024a,b) aligns student and teacher distributions using objectives such as reverse KL, Fisher divergence, and moment matching. FGM aligns velocity fields but considers only Gaussian forward processes (Huang et al., 2024), where its objective reduces to Fisher divergence (Zhou et al., 2024b). TDM (Luo et al., 2025) has shown strong few-step performance by learning partial denoising at each step. Our VA-TDM unifies score distillation, Fisher divergence, and moment matching while yielding new distillation objectives. Combined with transition-aware online field learning, it achieves state-of-the-art few-step performance. Generative adversarial networks.. Early GAN research achieved strong results on domain-specific datasets (Karras et al., 2020, 2021; Reed et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017), while it has been effectively extended these successes to ImageNet (Brock et al., 2019; Russakovsky et al., 2015; Sauer et al., 2022). However, training instability and limited scalability remain key challenges. Large-scale text-to-image GANs still rely on convolutional architectures with complex designs (Kang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025), and scaling transformer-based GANs remains difficult (Jiang et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2021). Adversarial Flow Models (AFM) (Lin et al., 2026) train many-step flow-matching models through an adversarial game in velocity space, requiring discriminator Jacobian-vector products (JVPs). Our work also formulates an adversarial game in velocity space, but targets few-step distillation and avoids expensive JVP computation. 6. Conclusions We introduced Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), unified framework that guides distillation through velocity fields constructed from the students sampling process. By separating the choice of field from the generator update, VAD connects score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, clarifies MMDs heuristic updates, and derives new training objectives. Building on this framework, VA-TDM combines dual-form supervision with transition-aware online velocity learning to supervise partial denoising along few-step student trajectories, without adding inference cost. Experiments across text-to-image and text-to-video generation demonstrate VA-TDM consistently achieves state-of-the-art four-step performance. VA-TDM also scales effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3, outperforming Fast-H3 in human evaluation and substantially narrowing the perceptual quality gap to the many-step teacher. These results highlight the value of our work, establishing VAD as principled foundation for designing effective few-step distillation methods.
